performers: Carl Sandburg, narrator; New York Philharmonic; André Kostelanetz
intro: Copland’s Lincoln Portrait, with Carl Sandburg, Lincoln’s biographer, as narrator and André Kostelanetz, who commissioned the piece, conducting. Before the narration begins, the orchestra plays two nineteenth-century tunes in a slow opening section and a faster middle section.

cues.title: Slow opening section
cues.text: The slow opening, the first of the work’s three sections, is played by the orchestra before the narrator speaks. In his note for the Boston Symphony’s 1943 performance, Copland described this part as a portrait of Lincoln’s fatality and gentleness. The orchestra plays broad phrases before the narrator names Lincoln.
cues.evidence: Copland’s note for the Boston Symphony’s 1943 performance, reproduced by the LA Phil, describes the first of the work’s three sections. https://www.laphil.com/works/lincoln-portrait
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Commission and first performance, 1942
cues.text: André Kostelanetz, the conductor of this recording, commissioned the work during the Second World War. He also conducted its first performance, with the narrator William Adams and the Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra, on 14 May 1942.
cues.evidence: Commission and première: Aaron Copland Fund work catalogue. The Columbia MS 6040 sleeve identifies Kostelanetz as conductor of this recording. https://www.aaroncopland.com/works/lincoln-portrait/

cues.title: Quick middle section
cues.text: In his 1943 programme note Copland described the quick middle section as a sketch of Lincoln’s times. He used Camptown Races and the ballad Springfield Mountain in the piece and treated both tunes freely.
cues.evidence: Copland’s 1943 programme note names both songs, explains their free treatment and identifies the quick middle section as a sketch of Lincoln’s times. https://www.laphil.com/works/lincoln-portrait
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final section with narrator
cues.text: In the final section a narrator speaks over the orchestra. In his note for the Boston Symphony’s 1943 performance, Copland called the orchestra’s task “a simple but impressive frame about the words of Lincoln himself”. On the Columbia recording the narrator is Carl Sandburg.
cues.evidence: The quotation is from Copland’s note for the Boston Symphony’s 1943 performance, reproduced by the LA Phil. The Columbia sleeve identifies Carl Sandburg as the narrator. https://www.laphil.com/works/lincoln-portrait
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Carl Sandburg, Columbia LP
cues.text: Carl Sandburg was a poet and a biographer of Lincoln. Columbia printed his name beside the work’s title on this LP, with Kostelanetz conducting the New York Philharmonic.
cues.evidence: Original Columbia Masterworks MS 6040 sleeve: credits and paragraph identifying Sandburg as poet and Lincoln biographer. https://archive.org/download/lp_a-lincoln-portrait-new-england-triptych_andr-kostelanetz-the-new-york-philharmonic/lp_a-lincoln-portrait-new-england-triptych_andr-kostelanetz-the-new-york-philharmonic_djvu.txt

cues.title: Final section, narrator
cues.text: Copland gives the final section to a speaking voice, with passages drawn from Lincoln’s speeches and writings. The work is scored for narrator and orchestra.
cues.evidence: The Aaron Copland Fund catalogue specifies narrator and orchestra, with text arranged from Lincoln’s speeches; Copland’s three-section account explains the final section’s framing purpose. https://www.aaroncopland.com/works/lincoln-portrait/ ; https://www.laphil.com/works/lincoln-portrait
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

composer.background:
The Copland family lived above and beside their department store on Washington Avenue in Brooklyn. Aaron, born on 14 November 1900, was the youngest of Sarah and Harris Copland’s five children. His parents were Russian-born Jewish immigrants, and everyone in the family helped in the shop. His sister Laurine gave him his first piano lessons. When he wanted professional lessons, his parents let him find a teacher and agreed to pay. By 1917 he was crossing the Brooklyn Bridge to study harmony and counterpoint with Rubin Goldmark.

At Fontainebleau in 1921 a friend persuaded him to sit in on Nadia Boulanger’s harmony class. She became his composition teacher, and the year he had planned to spend abroad stretched to three. In Paris he encountered Stravinsky’s music and heard the latest concert works. Boulanger took him to meet Serge Koussevitzky, who was about to take over the Boston Symphony Orchestra. After the visit Koussevitzky commissioned a symphony with Boulanger herself as organ soloist.
